title: Unable to access certain sites on Chrome using Exit Nodes
body: ### What is the issue? I am using Tailscale's Exit Nodes my macOS device. While using the Exit Nodes I am unable to access certain websites. I am getting an ERR_CONNECTION_RESET error on Chrome. This error only occurs on Chrome and the same website can be accessed over Safari. Few others use Tailscale in our company and they do not seem to have this problem. It selectively occurs on certain devices is my suspicion. Bug report - BUG-6d2218208b897581dbf3fbb18f1df079c6904f36c5046d770be2e42a4199d3a4-20230919210540Z-903996c7ac93c724 ### Steps to reproduce I am not certain as this could be related to Tailscale-Chrome settings. ### Are there any recent changes that introduced the issue? This is my first time using Exit Nodes. ### OS macOS ### OS version Ventura 13.5.2 ### Tailscale version Version 1.48.2 (macsys) ### Other software Avast AV ### Bug report BUG-6d2218208b897581dbf3fbb18f1df079c6904f36c5046d770be2e42a4199d3a4-20230919210540Z-903996c7ac93c724

comments.author: participant1
comments.body:
Around the time of the bugreport we notice IPv6 connections timing out.
```
2023-09-19 21:00:57.470791 +0000 UTC: open-conn-track: timeout opening (TCP [fd7a:115c:a1e0:ab12:q:r:s:t]:64839 => [2607:q:r:s:t::53]:443) to node [+7/Uc]; online=yes, lastRecv=9s
2023-09-19 21:00:57.612709 +0000 UTC: open-conn-track: timeout opening (TCP [fd7a:115c:a1e0:ab12:q:r:s:t]:64841 => [2607:q:r:s:t::5f]:443) to node [+7/Uc]; online=yes, lastRecv=9s
```

The destination IPv6 address ends in :0000:0000:0000:0053, which means these are almost certainly DNS-over-HTTPS connections to some DNS server. The full IPv6 address doesn't match a DNS service I am familiar with.

comments.author: participant1
comments.body:
> This error only occurs on Chrome and the same website can be accessed over Safari

So far as I can tell:
- Chrome is using its built in DNS resolver. The IPv6 DNS server address it is sending to reverse resolves to a *.1e100.net name, so it is a Google DNS server. I assume it is a non-publicized set of IP addresses which Chrome uses.
- Chrome is not falling back to try IPv4.

Can I ask what the exit node is, and in particular is it a Linux system with a TUN interface or is it something else?
https://tailscale.com/kb/1177/kernel-vs-userspace-routers/ means that an exit node running macOS/Windows/Android/etc is terminating the TCP connection on the tailnet and making a new outgoing TCP connection. This might be fooling Chrome into thinking that IPv6 works, when it only actually works to reach the exit node and fails on the public side of the exit node.

comments.author: participant1
comments.body:
For the benefit of people finding this issue later:
- Linux with a /dev/net/tun device is able to do kernel forwarding.
- Linux with no TUN interface, as is often the case with containers, is started with `tailscale --tun=userspace-networking` and performs routing functions in userspace, so the limitations in https://tailscale.com/kb/1177/kernel-vs-userspace-routers/ apply.

----

We also have an internal support ticket, so I was able to look up the exit nodes. They are running Linux with a /dev/net/tun device, so they are doing packet routing.

We're still looking, but what we know so far is that Chrome is sending the DNS queries to an IPv6 address and it never falls back to IPv4. Usually it will fall back to IPv4 if IPv6 times out, so something is convincing Chrome to stick with IPv6.

comments.author: participant4
comments.body:
The second pcap looks similar to the first in that we see IPv6 destination unreachable responses from the exit node. This is to be expected as it looks like the exit node does not have external IPv6 connectivity. What's more interesting about the second pcap is that there are DNS queries for Google properties, so we can infer what Chrome is trying to connect with. 

Chrome is querying for both IPv4 (A) and IPv6 (AAAA) records simultaneously, and there are valid, well-formed answers arriving for both within the same millisecond. For the domain where IPv6 is failing, Chrome is sometimes communicating via (IPv4) QUIC/UDP, or not at all post-DNS response. Due to the encrypted nature of QUIC we can't understand when a QUIC connection is "reset".

Working under the assumption that the IPv4 QUIC connections are being reset, and not falling back to IPv4 TCP, can you try disabling QUIC in Chrome and report back on if the issue persists? Navigate to chrome://flags/ and change `Experimental QUIC protocol` from Default/Enabled => Disabled. I wouldn't consider this a fix, but it tests my current theory.

comments.author: reporter
comments.body:
Interesting! I applied the changes and it almost worked for a while. Everything was working fine for 10 minutes and soon after I relaunched my browser the issue was back again. I checked if the flags were set to disabled still after the Chrome re launch and it was disabled. 

Not sure how it was working one min and failed after I re launched Chrome.

comments.author: participant4
comments.body:
Establishing IPv6 connectivity through the exit node resolved the issue. Chrome was preferring IPv6, and seemingly able to establish a TCP stream via 3-way, so it deemed IPv6 was healthy/functional. There was a proxy in play that appeared to handshake with Chrome before it had successfully opened a stream with the true destination. So, Chrome would see an open stream, then it would be closed shortly after, but it wouldn't fall back to IPv4.

Very similar to https://github.com/participant5/participant5/issues/5425#issuecomment-1232259971, except we were not the problematic proxy this time.
